title: Workflow Organization
text: Open RStudio not R. You should see this window

title: Setup R
text:
Before doing anything with R, it is very important to first setup your workflow


Create a new folder on your Desktop and name it comm_106
::: {.os-pair} 
 :::

R and RStudio are different things and need to be installed separately. Once you do this, you won’t have to do it again.

R — the language itself.
RStudio — the app you’ll actually look at and type in.

They’re separate programs and you need both. R alone works but is unpleasant; RStudio without R won’t do anything.
Unfortunately, the links you’ll need to click on to download depend on whether you’re using Mac or Windows, and which version of macOS or Windows you’re running. You can make life easier by updating your macOS/Windows version to the most current version before installing anything.

title: Install R for Windows
text: Go to the R for Windows Installation site and click Download R for Windows. You must be running Windows 10 or higher.

title: Create, save R Markdown file
text:
Open RStudio



This should appear


Find the icon to make a new file on the top left, under the toolbar. It looks like a white rectangle with a green plus sign on it. Click on R Markdown



Create a new R Markdown document


A pop-up on installing packages will appear, let it run and wait for it to finish.



Installation pop up


Window for making new R Markdown document will appear, click on Create empty document




Installation pop up



Save this file (Command, S on Mac, Ctrl, S on Windows). 
Name it practice_01 – keep the .Rmd extension at the end. Save the file in your comm_106 folder, which lives on your Desktop.




Save and name file



In the future, you can find and work on practice_01.Rmd in your comm_106 folder.

title: Numeric, Logical, Character
text:
Character
A character is text wrapped in quotes, like “hello” or “5”. R treats it as words, not numbers, so you can combine, search, or change it, but you can’t do math with it.

title: Vectors and Vector Operations
text: We now know about the Numerics, Logicals, and Character classes; that we can use functions on these objects; and we can assign variable names to objects.

title: Vectors and Vector Operations
text:
Vectors
A vector is a set of values of the same type. You can think of it like a column on a spreadsheet. We can make a vector with the c() function.


practice_01.Rmd

::: {.cell autorun='false'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
num_vector <- c(1, 2, 3)
print (num_vector)

sus_vector <- c(1, "2", 3)
print (sus_vector)
```
:::

All the elements in a vector need to be the same datatype, there are some functions that work on entire vectors.
We can get the mean, or average, number of Red Bulls I drink every week for the last 6 weeks by using the mean() function.


practice_01.Rmd

::: {.cell autorun='false'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
redbulls_drank <- c(7, 6, 12, 8, 7, 2)
print (class(redbulls_drank))
print (mean(redbulls_drank)) 
```
:::

Note that every element in redbulls_drank is of the numeric type. We can also do things with vectors filled with characters. The toupper() function turns every character into uppercase.


practice_01.Rmd

::: {.cell autorun='false'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
redbull_flavor <- c("cherry", "lime", "apple", "strawberry") 
toupper(redbull_flavor)
```
:::

However, it wouldn’t make sense to try to get the mean of my favorite flavors. Nor would it make sense to try to uppercase numbers.


practice_01.Rmd

::: {.cell autorun='false'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
print (mean(redbull_flavor)) 
print (toupper(redbulls_drank))
```
:::

It also wouldn’t make sense to get the mean of the number of Red Bulls I drank and my favorite flavors.


practice_01.Rmd

::: {.cell autorun='false'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
redbull_comp <- c("cherry", "lime", "apple", "strawberry", 7, 6, 12, 8, 7, 2) 
print (mean(redbull_flavor)) 
```
:::

This doesn’t mean that numeric vectors can only use numeric vector functions, that logical vectors can only use logical vector functions, and so on. The length() function tells you how many elements are in a vector, and works on all kinds of vectors, and the unique() function tells you how many unique values are in a vector.


practice_01.Rmd

::: {.cell autorun='false'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
print (length(redbull_flavor))
print (length(redbulls_drank))
print (unique(redbull_flavor))
print (unique(redbulls_drank)) 
```
:::

You can also access a specific element in a vector based on its position. In redbull_flavor, “cherry” has a position of 1, “lime” has a position of 2, “apple” has a position of 3, and “strawberry” has a position of 4. We can refer to a specific element by: redbull_flavor[1], which is “cherry”


practice_01.Rmd

::: {.cell autorun='false'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
print (redbull_flavor[1])
print (redbull_flavor[2])
# Same concept for redbulls_drank 
print (redbulls_drank[1])
```
:::


Vector to Vector Operations
We can work with multiple vectors. We’ll make a new numeric vector that lists the number of cups of water I drank each week for the past 6 weeks.


practice_01.Rmd

::: {.cell autorun='false'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
waters_drank <- c(8, 6, 9, 4, 8, 0)
```
:::

We can get a new vector by adding redbulls_drank to waters_drank using the same numeric operation rules for numerics.


practice_01.Rmd

::: {.cell autorun='false'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
waters_drank + redbulls_drank 

# Subtraction
difference_vector <- waters_drank - redbulls_drank
```
:::
